prize_parts.citation: For incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and so transforming the analysis of who trades, how trade reallocates resources, and the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: Firm heterogeneity and selection replaced the representative-firm trade model with one in which trade liberalisation reallocates activity across firms and changes aggregate productivity. Melitz (2003) is the clear originator of the framework. Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exports versus FDI, and his wider role in new trade theory, turned it into a general research programme. The framework changed theory and the use of firm-level microdata. It also fed into quantitative trade, productivity measurement and macro and growth analysis of reallocation. It is now standard teaching and policy-evaluation material, and it has been tested against firm-level data for more than twenty years. Trade has not been recognised since 2008, so the timing is plausible. A two-person award keeps credit tight and defensible. Several members who rank B012 highly cite the same attribution logic (Melitz and Helpman, with Redding as a later quantitative contributor). Their agreement does not itself count as scientific merit. The case rests on the evidence on originality, scope and confirmation.
statement.case_against: Credit for the heterogeneous-firm agenda is broader than the ballot names suggest. Bernard and Jensen documented the exporter-premia facts, and Eaton and Kortum built a parallel, closely related framework. A Melitz-Helpman prize therefore risks leaving out real contributors, and Redding's quantitative extensions are arguably substantial. Helpman also appears in B007, so honouring him here forecloses, or complicates, recognising the political-economy-of-protection work. Finally, the welfare conclusions of the quantitative versions depend on modelling assumptions.

responses.point: Strömberg also ranks B012 first. He limits the prize to Helpman and Melitz, treats Redding's quantitative and spatial work as more derivative of the core insight, and flags Bernard, Jensen and Eaton-Kortum as possible credit claimants.
responses.response: I agree on the two-person scope and on Redding. I would qualify the word 'derivative'. Redding's quantitative and spatial extensions are important, but they build on a core insight that is already well defined and confirmed. I also share the worry about the omitted empirical and parallel-theory contributors. That worry is a real attribution risk for the Committee, not a reason to widen the prize beyond the ballot's credited names. A citation about firm selection and reallocation as the core mechanism handles the risk better than adding a third name.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B007 (Grossman and Helpman, trade policy and political economy of protection) first. He cites clean two-person attribution and very high maturity, and he notes that Helpman's overlap with B012 may push the Committee to frame the award differently.
responses.response: The attribution of B007 is cleaner than that of B012, and I do not dispute that. My reservations are about breadth and testability. Andersson himself notes that the empirical support for the lobbying model's precise predictions is mixed. The firm-heterogeneity framework has been confirmed on microdata and has spread into macro, productivity and growth work. That wider footprint is why I rank it higher. I would keep B007 as a coherent alternative for Helpman, but I would not combine the two, since that would credit Helpman twice in one award.

responses.point: Hassler ranks the New Keynesian framework (B021) first, with Woodford, Taylor and Calvo as the conceptual anchors. He argues that its practical influence is very large and that the framework has survived the 2021-23 inflation and zero-lower-bound episodes.
responses.response: I put B021 second in my opening and I still see its importance. But the attribution arguments from colleagues, including Fredriksson, Krusell and Strömberg, have weakened my confidence in any three-name selection from eight credited names. Any trio, mine included, omits major contributors, and I already had real doubt about Calvo and Gertler. Hassler's own list notes that Rotemberg and Clarida-Gali-Gertler fall outside the credited set. That is a more serious problem for B021 than for B012, where two names capture the core. I have therefore dropped B021 from my alternatives.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B022 first, with Autor and Hanson as the core of the China-shock work. He credits the identification strategies and the first-order importance of the questions, and he acknowledges that the task-model credit is partly diffuse and the long-run trade-shock effects are still debated.
responses.response: I take the B022 evidence seriously. I did not rank it in my opening, and the breadth of support among colleagues is a reason to revisit that, though it is not evidence of merit. On merit, the research designs are credible and the policy relevance is large. My reservations are the ones Teorell names. The task framework has origins outside the credited set, and the persistence and magnitude of the trade-shock effects are still contested. Whether the Committee gives the prize to two or three people is a real judgement call between Autor and Hanson alone and adding Dorn or Katz. On those grounds I keep B012 as my preference, and I name B022 as my first alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers to recognise Helpman through B007 (Grossman) instead of B012, since the two ballots overlap on him.
How to weigh Bernard-Jensen and Eaton-Kortum credit, which the ballot does not include.
Whether Redding should be added as a third laureate for the quantitative and spatial extensions.
Whether B022's attribution (Autor, Hanson, Dorn or Katz) and the contested persistence of the China-shock effects are resolved well enough to put it ahead of B012.
My attribution views come from general knowledge and the supplied openings, and I have not independently verified them.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent for the preferred B012 (Helpman and Melitz) from the supplied profile. My profile lists no collaboration with them. I do have professional connections to other ballots. Peter Klenow is a long-running co-author, relevant to B026, which is not in my configuration. Per Krusell (secretary) and John Hassler (chair) are frequent co-authors and IIES colleagues, and both rank other ballots. I have not adjudicated these connections.
